## C R I T I C A L F O RU M : C RU C I B L E S O F P OW E R

# The Anatomy of Soviet and Nazi Power: Crucibles of Power Forum

Jan Burzlaff

Cornell University Email: jb2825@cornell.edu

## Abstract

This lead article introduces the Crucibles of Power forum, highlighting Michael David-Fox’s groundbreaking study of Smolensk under Stalinist and Nazi rule. Crucibles of Power offers a model social history of occupation, weaving together Soviet and German sources, survivor testimonies, and decades of scholarship to dismantle binary frameworks of totalitarian theory. By reframing power as a fractured and negotiated process, David-Fox reveals how overlapping regimes shaped individual choices, collaboration, and violence. Key themes-such as ‘biographical logics,’ the entanglement of Nazi and Soviet systems, and the performative dimensions of fear, rumor, and denunciation-anchor this forum’s discussions by Jochen Hellbeck, Elena Osokina, and Anna Krylova, alongside David-Fox’s own response. Read against the present, this book warns how authoritarian regimes are assembled, naturalized, and remembered. The article argues that Crucibles of Power not only reshapes our understanding of Stalinism and Nazism but also calls for new comparative histories of violence, emotion, and survival across Eastern Europe.

Keywords: Stalinism; Nazism; Holocaust; social history; totalitarian theory

Michael David-Fox’s Crucibles of Power is a landmark intervention in one of the most fraught questions of twentieth-century history: how to understand the intersections of Stalinist and Nazi violence? David-Fox gives us something far more difficult—and far more necessary—than flattened comparisons and moral equivalency. His history inhabits the fractured landscapes of Smolensk and the surrounding Smolensk region, an urbanregional world caught between two regimes and a crucible of overlapping state-building projects, ideological improvisation, and violence both enacted and absorbed from below. Drawing on decades of historiography and archival mastery, Crucibles of Power refuses the binary scaffolding of totalitarian theory, bringing full circle the Cold War historiography that Smolensk helped birth. The famed Smolensk Archive—captured by the Nazis, then the Americans—offered western historians an unprecedented window into Soviet governance and party life. Merle Fainsod drew on this trove in Smolensk under Soviet Rule (1958), producing a foundational study that portrayed the Soviet regime as both dysfunctional and centralized.1 Yet the archive’s partial scope and its silence on wartime experiences obscured as much as it revealed. Crucibles of Power builds on this legacy but moves far

The stakes of this book are not merely academic—which is why I convened this forum. With contributions from Jochen Hellbeck, Elena Osokina, and Anna Krylova, this forum brings together scholars who have transformed our understanding of Soviet society.3 I am deeply grateful for their incisive contributions and for Michael David-Fox’s thoughtful response. Crucibles of Power demands our attention not only because it stitches two regimes intoasinglehistoricalfabric,unravelingthethreadsofcontinuityandruptureintwentiethcentury eastern Europe. It is also a guide to what social history—and the study of eastern Europe writ large—can offer in an age of resurgent authoritarianism and politicized memory.4 The power of Crucibles of Power lies in its refusal to close the moral ledger, to impose simple binaries, or to deliver narrative closure. This is a book that demands a reckoning, not just with the past, but with how we continue to write it.

The Fractured Reality of Power

One of Crucibles of Power’s most lasting contributions is its redefinition of power as a social process. Michael David-Fox resists the urge to frame Stalinist and Nazi authority as totalizing structures, revealing how power in Smolensk was fractured, improvised, and constantly negotiated. David-Fox traces this arc from the Smolensk Affair of 1928—a regional scandal-turned-purge that revealed the performative dimensions of Stalinist justice—to the political cleansing that followed Soviet reoccupation in 1943 and beyond. In this world, repression ricocheted: the same Soviet bureaucrat purged in 1937 reappears as a Nazi collaborator in 1941, and a partisan commander who hunted Germans in 1943 is installed as a Soviet functionary in 1944, wielding the same instruments of fear he once opposed. Few figures illustrate this better than Boris Menshagin, the Soviet defense lawyer turned Naziappointed mayor who embodies the structural product of overlapping regimes. Power, for him and many others, was warped by proximity to danger, reshaped with each front line, and refracted through choices made at desks, in barracks, and behind kitchen doors. This reframing decisively breaks with three major paradigms. First, it puts Cold Warera totalitarian models to rest, replacing top-down control with a porous, adaptive matrix of governance.5 David-Fox builds on traditions of political and institutional history— Stephen Kotkin’s work on power, Jan T. The analysis of bezvlastie—the power vacuum in the wake of the Nazi invasion—captures this paradox brilliantly. In this moment of shattered sovereignty, the old Stalinist strategies of rumor, bribery, and opportunism did not disappear—they metastasized. Second, the book moves past the carefully staged dualism of Stalinism and Nazism, which were rarely allowed to bleed into one another.7 The Smolensk Affair thus appears as a precedent: local power was reshuffled through staged revelations, performative justice, and denunciation networks—tools later echoed in Nazi occupation and re-Sovietization alike. Third, David-Fox offers a necessary corrective to Timothy Snyder’s Bloodlands: Europe between Hitler and Stalin, which mapped overlapping violence but left the machinery of rule at the local level—its petty rivalries, improvisations, and local instabilities—largely untouched.8 David-Fox’s strength lies in replacing abstractframeworkswithwhat one could callasocialhistoryofentanglement.InSmolensk, Nazi and Soviet systems overlapped, echoed, and contaminated one another. What we are given is a rare narrative: a multi-regime history of Soviet coercion, Nazi improvisation, and ambiguous moments of fear, ambition, and adaptation. For this alone, and for rejecting revisionist accounts that either downplay Soviet violence or reframe collaboration as nationalist virtue, we owe David-Fox a rare kind of gratitude.9

Yet in my view, the book’s best conceptual contribution is the notion of “biographical logics.” Rather than probing whether people had agency, David-Fox asks how they used the situational agency available to them: how decisions emerged not from the classic liberal notions of free will or pure constraint, but from prior affiliations, material needs, and the changing horizons of possibility.10 Take the Maslennikov family: three siblings, raised under the same roof, end up on opposite sides of the war: one a partisan, one a translator for the Germans, and one an NKVD agent. Another is Isaak Breitman, a Jewish communist who survives the Holocaust by posing as a Ukrainian and entering Nazi auxiliary service. These are stories of improvisation in a world where no decision was made in isolation, and every path carried the weight of past ties and uncertain futures. Crucibles of Power implicitly critiques the deterministic tendencies of recent work, which rightly emphasizes the impact of Soviet rule on wartime behaviors but often risk portraying those influences as fixed.11 Instead, David-Fox tells a story not of cause and effect, but of personnel, memory, and opportunism

Violence as a System

As a historian of the victims of mass violence, I also read Crucibles of Power through a second lens: the voices that flinch from the archive—Jewish survivors, women navigating coercion, and civilians caught in the blur between denunciation and complicity. What I found was an excellent mapping of calibrated and reenacted violence: a milkmaid testifies that a veterinarian has sabotaged a cow’s milk yield (Ch. 3); gas vans roll into Smolensk to test their killing efficiency before deployment to Auschwitz (Ch. 5); and women who exchanged sex for food or safety are later branded “German mattresses” and executed by partisans (Ch. 8). The book’s insistence on scenes like these gives voice—however belated—to those who experienced it. David-Fox brings extraordinary precision to the local workings of total war, tracing how individuals became agents of harm, witnesses to it, or its collateral, and how the categories between them could collapse. The Holocaust is thus treated with exceptional clarity. The liquidation of the Smolensk ghetto on July 15–16, 1942, is framed as central to the regime’s vision of “order.” In Smolensk, the extermination of Jews was not a distinct policy running parallel to antipartisan warfare—it was fused with it.12 Chapter 6 chillingly reconstructs how Wehrmacht officers came to see Jews and Soviet resisters as a single, indistinguishable enemy: the Judeo-Bolshevik partisan. In this logic, ghetto liquidation, rural massacres, and counterinsurgency became mutually reinforcing.13 The death marches from Viazma and Roslavl—where prisoners were shot, starved, or abandoned—underscore the geographic reach and logistical brutality of German rule. We also see how Nazi authorities co-opted local forms of repression, such as Komandanty ulits (street commandants) and politsai (auxiliary police) as inheritors of Soviet surveillance routines. The line between racial colonization and extermination policy was so thin as to become meaningless, and it is one of the book’s core merits that it tells this story outside major Holocaust narratives.14

Futures of Comparison, Fields ofViolence

What emerges, then, is not a story of regime succession but of layered rule: a form of governance shaped not just by ideology or repression, but by improvisation, institutional memory, and the entanglement of violence across time. It is a vision of Soviet and Nazi power as uneven terrain, one that resists neat comparisons but invites new ones. What might such a framework reveal in territories of old Soviet rule, the multiethnic borderlands annexed after 1939, and contested sovereignty in interwar Poland, wartime Yugoslavia, or postwar Romania?15 I believe these questions will allow us to reevaluate Soviet rule under conditions of collapse, occupation, and return. Like Anna Hájková, who has called for a history of sex work under Nazi rule, David-Fox invites us to take these economies seriously.16 In occupied Smolensk, to share a bed with a German could mean food, heat, and survival; but it also meant visibility, rumor, and sometimes execution. Clearly, the performative dimensions of violence—photographs of rape,stagedkillings, mass spectacles—were not limited to the front lines.17 They spilled into homes, village squares, and postwar memories, calling for more case studies and comparative research. What gives Crucibles of Power its particular weight for readers of this journal, however, is its sensitivity to how Stalinist violence shaped wartime events. The 1930s were a training ground: denunciation networks, purges, and ideological performance created habits that outlived the regime. The Deduška Regiment, composed of up to 80% escaped Soviet POWs, is emblematic: an anti- Nazi unit born from Stalinist militarism. We now need systematic comparisons of this mechanism—subtle, cumulative—for communities across Soviet territories and beyond. To what extent were initial pro-German sympathies and help offered to persecuted minorities shaped by prior experiences under Soviet rule? Did other cities and regions with prior exposure to Stalinist violence, collectivization, and purges in the 1930s see similar or different patterns of flight, compliance, or refusal?18 This book on Smolensk, a provocative lens chosen for analytical leverage, calls for collaborative and interdisciplinary efforts to trace these patterns of violence across space and time.19 Finally, it invites us to write comparative histories of emotions.20 Fear is everywhere in this book: fear of denunciation, of silence, of being left behind or pulled in. In an article just published, I argue that fear was both scar tissue and armor in the multiethnic Polish borderlands (kresy).21 David- Fox offers a solid foundation for future histories of fear, hope, shame, and desire as agents of violence lived, remembered, and reproduced. With Crucibles of Power, we are no longer asked to compare from above, but rather from below, from within, and from the middle of a fractured world. Ultimately, David-Fox offers a quiet yet powerful warning about authoritarianism in our own century. Read against the present, the book shows us that such regimes rarely impose themselves fully formed; they are assembled, inhabited, and naturalized through denunciation cultures, bureaucratic improvisation, and the recycling of personnel. With archival dexterity and narrative control—slow, precise history in the service of difficult truths— David-Fox has written an urgent book about multidirectional entanglement. His Smolensk is a city where oppression and resistance coexisted, where victims could become perpetrators, and where ideology often bent under the weight of pragmatism. For all scholars of Eastern Europe, Crucibles of Power is a mandatory read: a devastatingly intelligent, layered, and much-needed intervention in our understanding of Stalinism, Nazism, and the lived experiences of World War II. It is not an easy book, nor should it be. Some histories should leave us unsettled.

# Neither Perpetrators nor Victims: Civilians Facing Mass Violence

Jan Burzlaff

Review of: Mary Fulbrook, Bystander Society: Conformity and Complicity in Nazi Germany and the Holocaust (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2023). 488 pp. (hardback) USD 34.95 ISBN: 978-0-197-69171-7. M

ary Fulbrook’s  Bystander Society  is a milestone in the study of the Holocaust in particular, and the role of ci­ vilians in the face of genocide and mass violence in gen­ eral. It is the first book that systematically examines all those who, in Nazi Germany between 1933 and 1945, neither directly perpetrated violence nor were targeted for persecution.1 To date, that vague definition has reflected more the lack of in-depth studies than the historical record. Fulbrook convincingly tackles the making of this group, comprising the vast majority of non-Jewish Germans between 1933 and 1945. Standing by acts of discrimination and violence towards Jews — not acting, not protesting, not speaking up — became socially required, Fulbrook argues, and participating in such acts was wide­ ly tolerated, if not openly encouraged. By not acting, not speaking up, and going along with new, racialized norms, which Nazi authorities ferociously enforced but that they also quickly adopted, at least pub­ licly, most ordinary Germans contributed to the Holocaust. Based on personal accounts, Bystander Society is an excellent book not only for its key insights into the social conditions that, unwillingly but always in­ exorably, paved the way for what happened after 1939. The book is also a warning, demonstrating how a repressive state undoes existing ties and destroys the very possibility of social interactions from the bottom up.

To make her case, Fulbrook explores the rich collection of some 250 personal accounts, ‘My life in Germany before and after January 30, 1933’. Probing what was an essay competition run by three Harvard pro­

fessors in 1939-1940, and which is now available at Harvard’s Houghton Library, Fulbrook avoids the benefits of hindsight by chronicling how these émigrés perceived the growing racialization of social identities after 1933. Indeed, most Germans were neither perpetrators nor vic­

In the absence of direct acts of harm on the one hand, and generalized social exclusion on the other, scholars often relied upon the static, one-sizefits-all label of bystander that was popularized by Raul Hilberg’s 1992 book.2 Yet the term captures neither the changes in behaviours nor the range of personal implications in Nazism.3 Bystander Society makes the best case to date for distinguishing between degrees of complici­ ty, from willing facilitation and functional complicity to constrained conformity. The twelve chapters, chronologically organized, capture well this threefold process, from fearful consent and passivity in the early 1930s (part I, ‘The Slippery Slope: Social Segregation in Nazi Ger­ many’, pp. 27–170) and constrained conformity and willing facilitation after 1935, to, lastly, what she dubs functional conformity, defined as all behaviours that furthered Nazi policies (part II, ‘The Expansion of Violence at Home and Abroad’, pp. 173–368). While most chapters dwell

on Germany, chapter 9 probes these aspects for Lithuania and Latvia (pp. 268–309). Up to 1935, the speed of this process depended on pre-1933 relationships, social class, and status. The 1935 Nuremberg Laws repre­ sented an important milestone because they codified the racial distinc­ tion upon which ‘Aryans’ were expected to act and perform. Racialized differences, invented and enforced from the top-down, and however despised in private, had become a public reality.

After 1935, seemingly small shifts in private — such as not invit­ ing a friend to a social event — evolved alongside, and often followed, public performances of conformity. Like venom, the racial difference proclaimed from above slowly penetrated the local fabric and reshaped the private sphere, a depth rarely acknowledged after 1945 under the umbrellas of fear, ignorance, or inner resistance. Here, Fulbrook con­ nects Bystander Society to her 2018 book on postwar justice (or injustice), winner of the 2019 Wolfson Prize.4 ‘Far greater numbers,’ she astutely notes, ‘may never have truly acknowledged the degree to which they had become contaminated by their involvement in Nazism, even when challenged more explicitly in differing contexts after the war’ (p. 383). By the time the war broke out in 1939, and the victims had disappeared

Considering bystanding as a social process allows Fulbrook to make three contributions that are particularly relevant for readers of this journal. First and foremost, we ought to overcome any remain­ ing temptation to explain conduct in Nazi Germany and other cas­ es of mass violence through the sole lens of motivations and beliefs. Whereas scholars traditionally explained behaviours by examining

belief systems — or what appeared as such to observers then and to­ day — personal accounts point to many contradictions, shaped by often inaccessible inner worlds.6 Yet, as Fulbrook shows, one acted upon a public script, then talked oneself into and, more often than not, made a truce with the performance not simply because of the fear of repression and standing out, but because there were considerable benefits, mate­ rially and socially, to moulding oneself on what was expected. Such behaviours 'certainly both hurt the victims and actively assisted in the process of separating out communities along lines desired by the Nazi regime. Nor can it be brushed away in terms of “only obeying orders” (p. 111). The process was both insidious and subtle.’ Using the notion of ‘normal community’, adopted from sociologist Erving Goffman, Ful­

brook moves beyond the old debates about the origins of public accept­ ance of Nazism rooted in either imposed terror or willing support.7;8 ‘From the perspective of the muddled middle’, Fulbrook sums up, ‘the

mere fact of such widespread outward conformity—for whatever range of reasons—led to the perceived fiction of unity and consensus, making it even harder for wavering souls to risk standing out from the crowd or to challenge dominant views’ (p. 395). The latter conveniently helped solve any arising or remaining moral conflicts. Thus, most did not so much ‘learn to hate’ than ‘to comply, to conform, to demonstrate in daily behaviours identification with the dominant, “racially” defined national community’ (pp. 377-378).

The book’s second major contribution lies in the refutation of ‘by­ standers’ and other labels, instead suggesting a wider spectrum of con­ formity and compliance that can be fruitfully applied to other cases. While universally applauded, Michael Rothberg’s expression of the ‘implicated subject’ does not capture this spectrum of involvement and

complicity with Nazi racism, as Fulbrook’s book makes clear.9 Simi­ lar generalizations have been made about other contexts of occupied Europe — think only of Robert Paxton’s debated assertion that most non-Jewish French people were ‘functional collaborators’.10 Clearly, most Germans were not perpetrators, but they were not passive by­ standers either: passivity was a learned mechanism of socially accept­ able behaviours. This also renders moot the question of lack of knowl­ edge, a classic line of defence after the war and arguably present in the literature until the 2010s.11 Pretending not to piece together various el­ ements about the fate of Jews made one’s own perceived powerlessness much easier. A fruitful line of inquiry, Fulbrook suggests, tracks what ordinary people made of such knowledge in specific contexts, which can now be applied to social histories of state-sponsored discrimina­ tion and persecution.

The third and related contribution is the exploration of social pat­ terns in the 1930s without foreshadowing the war years. As a historian of victims of mass violence, I applaud her effort to foreground personal accounts and to make out patterns.12 Instead of focusing on individu­ al perpetrators, Fulbrook describes this process from conformity to compliance at the communal level, with considerable regional varia­ tions — from the southern village of Gailingen to Hamburg and Berlin. Future studies should further refine this shift from outward conform­ ity to functional complicity. To what extent did this shift depend on social patterns among non-Jewish Germans and pre-1933 factors, such as religion, social class, or voting patterns? Future comparisons will yield deeper insights into this process of racialization of local, regional, and national identities.

In the same vein, the notions of performance, roleplay, and public script all deserve more attention in considering this segregation pro­ cess. Since 99.9 percent of Germans did not rescue Jews in the sense of a long-term commitment, scholars interested in small gestures of help, food, and sympathy that mattered so much in the cracks of a bystand­ er society will find many avenues for exploration. Arguably, inaction, looking away, and silence could also mean fleeting or ever-growing opposition to Nazism — keeping silent about Jews hidden in a cellar or renting out an apartment to strangers, thus offering protection without intending it, at least initially. The more we move into Eastern Europe and the longer the war went on, the more relevant the idea of function­ al complicity seems to become, which calls to refine further various forms of complicity.13 This effort must be collective, interdisciplinary — engaging all kinds of disciplines studying violence — and finally in­

clude the vast collections of video testimonies recorded since the late 1970s, amounting to some 20 years of uninterrupted listening.14 The

book’s thick descriptions will be a treasure trove for all those interest­ ed in examining (anew) cases of state-sponsored violence.

In sum, Bystander Society tells a crucial story of falling in line with state-sponsored discrimination, new norms on race violently enforced but also quickly adopted, whatever the personal beliefs and motivations. Aware of the continuing importance of studying this racialization and

segregation process at hand, Fulbrook rightly does not shy away from making connections with contemporary events, from Derek Chau­ vin’s trial to American election denialism and recurring, disparaging remarks by Donald J. Trump. Perhaps most frightening to a reader to­ day, certainly to this reviewer, is the fact that ‘many Germans found it possible to maintain a sense of their own moral integrity while at the same time furthering the Nazi cause by public conformity’ (p. 91). The pace with which this muddled middle did so after 1933 remains indeed stunning. This excellent book is a milestone in understanding civilian responses to mass violence.

Jan Burzlaff is a Postdoctoral Associate in the Program of Jewish Studies and the Department of Near Eastern Studies at Cornell University. As a historian, he is committed to bringing to life the contingency and com­ plexity of human behaviours in extremis, particularly the responses of Jews and non-Jews between 1939 and 1945. As cases of mass violence across the globe are again on the rise, his scholarship aims to yield a fuller understanding of civilian responses to persecution.
